sentences.text: The third day was the longest.
They started before dawn.
They had to make it into Porto before nightfall.
Senhor Fonseca said the river got busier as you approached the city — big tour boats, motor barges — and it was harder to sail an old boat in traffic.
Yara worked her rope.
She watched the wind.
She was tired.
Her hands were sore.
But she was — she noticed — she was actually helping.
She was actually part of the sailing.
Senhor Fonseca gave small instructions and she did them without needing to be told twice.
It felt good.
At about eleven that morning, Senhor Fonseca called her over to the stern.
He said, "Yara.
I want you to try the oar." She looked at him.
She said, "Really?" He said, "Really.
For maybe five minutes.
It is not hard here — the river is straight, the current is steady.
I will stand next to you.
But I want you to feel it.
So you know what it is.
So that when you are older, you can say — I steered a rabelo down the Douro.
Come."
So Yara stood at the back of the boat.
She put both her hands on the long wooden oar.
Senhor Fonseca stood beside her but did not touch the oar.
He said, "Feel the current on it.
Do you feel the pull." "Yes." "Now — the boat wants to drift a little to the right.
See where the bow is going.
Push the oar left.
Just a little.
Just a small motion." Yara pushed.
The boat responded.
It began to correct.
"Good," said Senhor Fonseca.
"Now hold it there.
Do not overcorrect.
Small movements.
Small." Yara held.
The boat sailed straight.
She steered for maybe ten minutes.
It was harder than it looked.
The oar was heavy.
The current was strong.
You had to hold your body against it.
But she did it.
She kept the boat straight.
Senhor Fonseca watched her the whole time.
When he took the oar back, he said, quietly, "You did well, Yara.
A person who has never steered a boat before does not usually keep a boat that straight.
You listened.
That is what steering is.
Listening."
In the late afternoon they came around a wide bend and there it was — Porto.
The city rose steeply on the right bank, all colored buildings and red roofs.
On the left, the old port wine warehouses of Vila Nova de Gaia.
The huge double-decker Dom Luís I bridge stretched across the river.
There were dozens of boats now — tour boats, small motor launches, a few larger cruise boats.
Yara had never seen so many boats.
Senhor Fonseca sailed the rabelo carefully, staying close to the left bank, out of the way of the bigger traffic.
The port wine museum had a small dock on the Vila Nova de Gaia side.
As they approached, Yara could see her mother standing at the dock, waving.
Yara waved back.
Senhor Fonseca steered them slowly in.
He tied the boat up.
A group of museum people came to help — a woman with a clipboard, two workers who would take the boat away for restoration.
They gave Senhor Fonseca some paperwork to sign.
He signed it.
Then he stepped off the boat.
He turned back to Yara.
He said, "Time to say goodbye.
Take a minute."
Yara stepped back onto the boat.
She walked its whole length slowly.
She touched the wooden mast.
She touched the ropes.
She stood at the front.
Then she went to the back and she stood at the steering oar for a moment with one hand on it.
She thought about her great-great-grandfather, whom she had never met and had never seen a picture of, who had stood in this exact spot with his hand on this same oar a hundred and thirty years ago.
She thought about all the trips his boat had made.
All the barrels of port it had carried.
All the years it had sat on their pier, quiet, waiting.
She said, quietly, to the boat, "Goodbye.
Thank you.
My great-great-grandfather sailed you.
My mother's mother's mother's father.
And now I have sailed you, on your very last trip.
I am glad you get to be in a museum.
I am glad you get to be seen.
I promise I will come and visit you.
I promise." Then she got off the boat.
Senhor Fonseca shook her hand — his real hand-shake, the adult kind.
He said, "Yara.
You are one of the sensible eleven-year-olds in Portugal.
I want you to remember something.
If in ten years or twelve years you decide you want to learn to sail one of these boats properly — write to me.
I am not too hard to find.
There are only three of us.
If you decide you want to learn — I will teach you.
It would be — it would be a good thing for me.
For me and for you both." He nodded.
He turned.
He walked away.
Yara stood on the dock with her mother.
Her mother said, "That is a very unusual offer, Yara." Yara said, "I know." Yara's mother said, "Are you going to write to him." Yara thought about it.
She thought about the three days.
About the current.
About steering.
About the small quiet man who had sailed eleven of these boats, and now twelve, and who was afraid the knowledge would die with him.
She said, "Yes.
When I am older.
I am going to write to him.
I want to learn." Her mother put her arm around her.
They stood on the dock for a while, watching.
In the distance, the museum workers were beginning to move the boat toward its new home.
The sun was setting over Porto.
The river was going gold.
